overview: Democrats won majorities in both the House and Senate in Tuesday's midterm elections, according to Wikipedia's news summary, and coverage this weekend turns to what that means for the White House and Congress. Overseas, a mass shooting in Kraków's Main Square left six people dead, Paraguay's president was removed from office amid a banking crisis, and Israeli politics is in flux over efforts to form a government. Markets had a rough week as a technology selloff and a steep drop in Japanese stocks weighed on investors.

stories.headline: Democrats win Congress; Senate Republicans weigh delaying leadership vote
stories.summary: Democrats won House and Senate majorities in Tuesday's midterm elections, though a few races were still uncalled on Saturday. House Democratic leaders said they will start the new Congress focused on health care and ending the Iran war, while several Senate Republicans are pushing to delay next week's party leadership elections.
stories.why_it_matters: A Democratic Congress can investigate the administration and block or reshape its legislative agenda, with health care costs and the Iran war named as early priorities.
stories.background: The 2026 midterms were the first national test of voters' views of President Trump's second term. Democrats needed to flip chambers held by Republicans; coverage describes a broad swing that included gains among Latino, young and independent voters. The new Congress is sworn in on Jan. 3. Senate Republican leader John Thune faces questions about the party's performance, and some colleagues want a review of the results before leaders are chosen.

facts.text: Democrats won sizable House and Senate majorities in the 2026 midterms, but exact margins were unclear because some races had not been projected as of Friday.
The Hindu reported that Democrats flipped both chambers, winning net seats in key battlegrounds and some Republican strongholds.
House Democratic leaders said health care and ending the Iran war are early priorities when the new Congress is sworn in on Jan. 3.
Bloomberg reported that several Senate Republicans want to delay next week's leadership elections, which could open the door to a challenge to John Thune.
The Washington Times reported Senate Republicans want a midterm review before leadership elections.
NPR reported that Americans under 30 voted decisively for Democrats, reversing some of the Republican gains with young voters in 2024.
The Hill reported that Hispanic voters helped Democrats, diminishing gains Trump made with Latino men, citing exit polling from BSP.

framing.note: Leads with Democratic majorities while stressing that some races remain uncalled.
Leads with Republican infighting and a possible post-mortem rather than the Democratic win.

stories.headline: Stephen Miller becomes White House chief of staff Monday
stories.summary: President Trump named deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller to replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff, effective Monday, Nov. 9. The move came days after Republican midterm losses, and some House Republicans reacted angrily, according to Fox News. Miller has pledged his devotion to the president, per The Guardian.
stories.why_it_matters: Miller has driven the administration's immigration crackdown, so his promotion signals that policy is likely to continue, and Democrats say they are preparing for a fight over it.
stories.background: Miller has been among Trump's longest-serving aides and the main architect of his immigration policies in both terms. Susie Wiles, the first woman to serve as chief of staff, is moving to Trump's political operation, according to the White House announcement. The change follows the midterms, in which voters gave Democrats control of Congress.

stories.headline: Trump asks Justice Department to investigate Democrats over alleged threats
stories.summary: On Saturday President Trump said he ordered the Justice Department to look into Democrats he accused of threatening administration officials and Republican donors, calling it 'extortion'. stories.background: Democrats won control of Congress this week and have discussed oversight of the administration, including possible impeachment of cabinet officials. Slotkin, a Michigan Democrat, said in January that she was under a Justice Department investigation over a video in which Democratic lawmakers urged troops to refuse illegal orders. Trump's latest statement did not come with details on any specific alleged crime in the digest summaries.

stories.headline: Judge to appoint ex-prosecutor to probe whether Trump lawyers misled court on golf course
stories.summary: U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes said Saturday she intends to appoint a former U.S. attorney in Washington to investigate whether administration officials misled the court about plans for the East Potomac golf course. The administration plans to close the course Nov. 15 to build a championship-level course, PBS reported.
stories.why_it_matters: It tests whether courts can hold government lawyers to account for statements they make in litigation, and it affects a public park in Washington.
stories.background: The administration plans to close East Potomac Golf Course and park and rebuild it. Reyes has been handling a lawsuit over the project. Late last month she said she would appoint a special master to examine whether Interior and Justice Department officials made misrepresentations, according to local reports. The reported core question is whether lawyers told the court no plans existed while Trump publicly announced a closing date.

The administration plans to close the course and park on Nov. 15 to build a 'world class, championship-level' course, PBS reported.
CNN reported the inquiry concerns possible ethical violations by administration lawyers.

stories.headline: Israel's president tasks Netanyahu rival Gadi Eisenkot with forming a government
stories.summary: President Isaac Herzog on Saturday chose former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, the strongest rival of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, to try to form Israel's next government after an inconclusive election. Eisenkot has up to six weeks to assemble a coalition, and he has so far declined to join forces with Arab parties whose support would give him a majority.
stories.why_it_matters: A change of leader in Israel would affect the war and ceasefire diplomacy, relations with Washington and the region, and who sets security policy for years. The coalition math is hard, so the outcome is still open.
stories.background: Israel held an election that produced no clear winner. Netanyahu's Likud won the most seats of any single party, but his religious-nationalist bloc fell short of a majority. Under Israeli law the president picks the lawmaker he judges most likely to build a coalition after consulting party leaders. Herzog said factions with 67 of 120 Knesset seats recommended Eisenkot and 46 recommended Netanyahu. The nominee gets 28 days, extendable by 14.

Eisenkot is a former army chief of staff and Netanyahu's strongest rival, and will have up to six weeks to form a coalition.

stories.headline: Six killed in Krakow market square shooting; Poland opens terrorism probe
stories.summary: A 24-year-old gunman with a semi-automatic rifle opened fire from a car near Krakow's Main Square on Saturday, killing six people and wounding more than a dozen before police shot and wounded him. Poland launched a terrorism investigation and declared two days of mourning after three more bodies were found at the suspect's home.
stories.why_it_matters: Mass shootings are rare in Poland, and the attack's far-right motive is raising security and political tension in a country already on edge over threats linked to Russia.
stories.background: Krakow's Main Square is one of Europe's busiest tourist and market areas. Poland has strict gun laws and has seen few mass killings. Authorities said the suspect was fascinated by far-right ideologies. Prime Minister Donald Tusk is leading the government's response.

facts.text: Six people were killed after a gunman opened fire in Krakow's Main Square area; he was shot by police and taken to hospital.
Authorities said the 24-year-old suspect used a semi-automatic rifle and was fascinated by far-right ideologies; Poland launched a terrorism probe.
Police confirmed the bodies found at the suspect's home were his parents and sister.
A Briton was among the dead, and Poland's defence minister called the attack an act of terror.
Poland began two days of mourning, and Tusk called on politicians not to exploit the incident.

stories.headline: Saudi strike near Sanaa kills dozens, then missiles damage Aramco tower in Riyadh
stories.summary: Houthi health officials said a Saudi air strike on a village near Sanaa on Saturday killed at least 33 people, mostly women and children. On Sunday Saudi Arabia said it intercepted missiles aimed at Riyadh's financial district, and falling debris damaged an Aramco administrative building with no injuries reported.
stories.why_it_matters: A renewed Saudi-Houthi exchange threatens civilians in Yemen and puts Gulf oil infrastructure and shipping back at risk, which can affect fuel prices.
stories.background: Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement controls Sanaa and has fought a Saudi-led coalition that backs the internationally recognized government for years. Saudi Arabia hosts the headquarters of Aramco, the state oil giant. The Houthis have periodically fired missiles and drones at Saudi territory. Saudi Arabia had not commented on the Saturday strike in early reports.

facts.text: The Houthi-run Health Ministry said airstrikes near Sanaa killed 33 people; the Houthis blamed Saudi Arabia, which had not commented.
Saudi Arabia's Energy Ministry said an Aramco administrative building in Riyadh was damaged by falling debris after an attempted attack, with no injuries.
France 24 reported the coalition intercepted two ballistic missiles headed for the financial district.
Syria denied reports that it would send thousands of troops to Yemen and Saudi Arabia, while saying military cooperation with the Saudis could expand.

stories.headline: Russian strikes hit Ukraine's power grid ahead of Abu Dhabi talks
stories.summary: Russian missiles and drones hit Kyiv-region energy facilities and a major bridge, wounding at least nine people. More than 600,000 customers were left without power, Ukrainian authorities said. Russian, Ukrainian and US delegations are due to meet in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday, and Russia is sending a higher-level team than before.
stories.why_it_matters: Winter attacks on power can mean outages and cold for millions of Ukrainians, and the talks are the clearest current chance of movement toward ending the war.
stories.background: Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022 and has repeatedly targeted the energy system before winter. The US is mediating talks that have stalled for months. Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov will join the Russian delegation for the first time. Germany's defence minister said Berlin cannot supply more Patriot systems for now.

stories.headline: Paraguay's Senate removes President Peña; he is charged over Ueno Bank collapse

The electoral commission was expected to announce final results on Sunday.

stories.summary: Pope Leo XIV drew about 40,000 people to a Mass in Uruguay on the second day of a 12-day tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, about three weeks after lung cancer surgery. He urged Catholics to be bridge builders and spoke about access to healthcare, then headed to Argentina, where tensions with President Javier Milei loom.
stories.why_it_matters: The tour tests the pope's health and signals the Church's stance on austerity and inequality in a region where Catholics are a large share of the population.
stories.background: Leo XIV is the first US-born pope. Uruguay is South America's most secular country. Argentina's Church is committed to social justice, which sits at odds with Milei's libertarian policies, per the NYT.

stories.headline: Tech and AI stocks sell off after Democrats win the midterms
stories.summary: US stocks fell sharply on Thursday, Nov. 5, led by technology and AI-related shares, after Democratic wins in the midterm elections raised investor worries about tougher scrutiny of AI data-center spending. Market data shows the S&P 500 fell about 4.4% that day, and the Nasdaq rebounded 1.1% on Friday while Japan's Nikkei fell about 6%. Investors are now reassessing AI-heavy positions and looking at out-of-favor markets in Asia.
stories.why_it_matters: AI stocks make up a large share of major index funds, so a drop in them hits most retirement accounts. It also signals that investors see policy risk for the AI buildout, which has been a main driver of stock gains.
stories.background: AI-related companies have driven much of the stock market's gains in recent years, with firms spending heavily on data centers and often borrowing to pay for it. Before the election, some AI companies had already faced weak earnings reports and higher borrowing costs. Democrats won a majority in both the House and Senate in the Nov. 3 midterms, according to Wikipedia's news summary. Some investors fear that this could mean limits on data-center construction and stricter regulation of AI.

facts.text: The S&P 500 fell about 4.4% on Nov. 5, its worst day since April 2025, according to a market-news report.
Reports tied the selloff to fears that a Democratic sweep could bring data-center moratoriums and heavier regulation of AI.

Bloomberg reported that the unwinding of the AI trade after the midterms is pushing investors back toward Chinese and Indian stocks and companies that benefit from easing inflation and trade tensions.
Meta sold $25 billion of corporate bonds on Election Day, which Bloomberg said highlights a changing landscape for tech debt.
Ark Invest CEO Cathie Wood told CNBC there is a 'wall of worry' gripping markets.

stories.headline: Hiring beats forecasts in October as inflation keeps the Fed in focus
stories.summary: US employers added 165,000 jobs in October, well above the roughly 65,000 economists expected, and the unemployment rate dipped to 4.1%, the Associated Press reported. With inflation running well above the Fed's 2% target, traders were reported to expect another quarter-point rate rise at the Fed's December meeting.
stories.why_it_matters: Strong hiring is good for job seekers, but it makes it less likely the Fed will cut rates soon, which keeps mortgage and credit-card rates high. The 30-year mortgage rate was 7.18% in the latest weekly reading.
stories.background: The Federal Reserve sets a short-term interest rate to try to hold inflation near 2% without causing job losses. Inflation has been rising, with the consumer price index up 3.7% over the year to September. According to the reporting, the Fed raised rates a quarter point in September, its first increase since 2023. The monthly jobs report from the Labor Department is one of the main data points the Fed watches.

facts.text: Employers added 165,000 jobs in October, versus about 65,000 expected by economists, and the unemployment rate fell to 4.1%.
Average hourly pay rose 0.4% in October from September, and annual inflation was 3.7% as of September.
About 75% of fed funds futures contracts priced in a quarter-point rate rise at the December meeting, according to CME Group data cited in a market report.

stories.headline: Berkshire Hathaway buys back $9.6 billion of stock as profit falls
stories.summary: Berkshire Hathaway reported third-quarter results on Saturday, Nov. 7. It spent about $9.6 billion repurchasing its own shares, more than double the prior pace, while profit declined. Weaker insurance results and smaller investment gains were cited.
stories.why_it_matters: Berkshire is a bellwether and a big holding in many index and retirement funds. Heavy buybacks signal that its management thinks its shares are cheap.
stories.background: Berkshire Hathaway is the conglomerate led by Warren Buffett and now run by CEO Greg Abel. It owns insurers such as Geico, railroads, utilities and a large stock portfolio. It reports results quarterly and often holds large amounts of cash, using buybacks only when it thinks the stock is undervalued. Insurance underwriting and investment gains are two main drivers of its profit.

facts.text: Berkshire spent about $9.6 billion on share buybacks in the third quarter.
Quarterly operating income fell 5.8% from a year earlier, the Financial Times reported, as insurance results slowed.
The Wall Street Journal reported net income fell 28% as investment gains shrank and insurance profits dropped.

stories.background: The US and Iran are in a conflict that has pushed up energy prices and inflation this year. Higher inflation has kept interest rates, and so mortgage rates, elevated. Oil is a major input to consumer prices through fuel and transport costs.

stories.headline: Federal judge orders city to give ICE names of Bronx shelter residents
stories.summary: A federal judge ruled on Nov. 7 that the Mamdani administration must give Immigration and Customs Enforcement the names of residents of a Bronx shelter, according to the Daily News and Gothamist. Gothamist reports the city had argued against the request. The digest summaries do not say whether the city will appeal.
stories.why_it_matters: The ruling bears on how far the city's shelter system can shield residents' information from federal immigration agents. Only left-leaning outlets in the digest covered it, so there is no right-leaning account to compare.
stories.background: New York City has sanctuary laws that limit local cooperation with federal immigration enforcement. A federal judge in Brooklyn dismissed a Trump administration suit challenging those laws in mid-October, as reported by several outlets. Mayor Zohran Mamdani has said ICE cannot enter city property without a judicial warrant. The new ruling concerns a request for shelter residents' names, a separate dispute from the sanctuary-law suit.

stories.headline: Arrest in Brooklyn jogger killing raises questions about Education Dept. vetting
stories.summary: The New York Post reports that an ex-NYPD officer who works as an elementary school educator was arrested in the killing of a jogger on a Brooklyn footpath. The Post also reports that Department of Education insiders are criticizing the agency's vetting of staff. Details come from the Post's reporting alone in the digest.

stories.headline: NYC fire deaths have nearly doubled this year after Sunset Park blaze
stories.summary: A Nov. 5 fire in a Sunset Park row house killed six people and injured nine, and the New York Times reports the city's fire deaths this year reached 86, nearly double last year's pace. Investigators are examining whether lithium-ion batteries played a role; the cause has not been confirmed. Mayor Mamdani has cited about 400 e-bike-related fires this year.
stories.why_it_matters: Fire deaths at this level affect anyone living in older or crowded housing, and charging e-bike batteries indoors is a common risk. The cause of the Sunset Park fire is still under investigation.
stories.background: Lithium-ion batteries in e-bikes and scooters have been a recurring cause of deadly fires in the city, and the FDNY has tied several deaths this year to them. A separate Bronx fire in the Patterson Houses on Oct. 28 killed three. Sunset Park is a densely populated Brooklyn neighborhood with many multi-family homes.

facts.text: The Times reports 86 fire deaths in the city this year, nearly double the prior year, after a Brooklyn fire that killed six people.
The Sunset Park fire killed six people and injured nine, according to reports by ABC7 and Scripps.

stories.headline: After midterms, Hochul weighs her next move as Republicans and the left take stock
stories.summary: Gov. Kathy Hochul won re-election convincingly, but the Times reports she is not discussing higher office. Democrats widened their hold on the state Legislature, while the Post reports Staten Island Republicans, including Rep. Nicole Malliotakis, held on. The Times says state Republicans have been blaming one another for their losses, and the Post reports the Democratic Socialists of America claimed credit for the results in a Manhattan rally.
stories.why_it_matters: Larger Democratic majorities in Albany shape state budget, housing and transit decisions that reach New York City. Accounts here come from the Times, a left-leaning outlet, and the Post, a right-leaning one, which stress different winners.
stories.background: Hochul faced a Republican challenger in the Nov. 3 midterms, in which Democrats won control of the House and Senate nationally, per the Post. In New York, Democrats expanded their control of the Legislature. Mayor Zohran Mamdani, elected last year, and the DSA are part of the party's left wing. The New York Sun reports Hochul and Mamdani marked the Democratic gains in Puerto Rico.

The Post reports Staten Island Republican candidates won while Democrats widened their control of the state Legislature.

markets.summary: U.S. stocks were mixed in the latest data: the S&P 500 fell 4.36% on its most recent reading (Nov. 5), while the Nasdaq rose 1.09% and the Dow slipped 0.46% a day later. Reporting links the pressure to a selloff in artificial-intelligence and tech shares after the midterms, and Japan's Nikkei dropped nearly 6% in a day. Bond yields fell as investors moved toward safer assets: the 10-year Treasury yield eased to 4.84% and the 30-year mortgage rate to 7.18%. Oil stays near $100 a barrel for U.S. crude, which keeps pressure on inflation, last measured at 3.72% a year.

movers.why: The 2-year Treasury yield fell 12 basis points as investors bought safer government debt; the digest does not give a single clear cause.

concept.explanation: A basis point is one-hundredth of a percentage point, so a 12-basis-point drop in a yield means it fell from, say, 4.58% to 4.46%. Traders use the term because small moves in interest rates matter a lot when applied to trillions of dollars of debt. Changes in yields flow into your wallet through mortgage rates, car loans and credit-card rates, which tend to follow Treasury yields up and down.
